summary: Canada's first national urban park, not a national park: a band of river valleys, forest, marsh and working farmland running from Lake Ontario north towards the Oak Ridges Moraine through Toronto, Markham, Pickering and Uxbridge. It is free, open every day of the year and reachable by subway, train and bus. Walk the wooded ridges above the Rouge River, look out over the valley in autumn colour, or paddle down to the largest marsh left in Toronto.

facts.suggestedTime: Half a day to a day

story: The Rouge River and its tributary, Little Rouge Creek, run through deep, wooded ravine valleys east of Toronto on their way to Lake Ontario. At Glen Eagles Vista a bluff above the river shows sandy brown layers laid down between 13,000 and 30,000 years ago, a record of thousands of years of climatic cooling and warming. The valleys open out at the lake into Rouge Marsh, the largest remaining wetland in the City of Toronto, and a sand beach at the river mouth.

The park lies at the northern edge of the Carolinian life zone, and its mix of slopes, soils and micro-climates gives it a diversity unusual so close to a city. Parks Canada counts more than 1,700 species here, including more than 1,000 plants, 247 birds, 73 fish, 44 mammals and 27 reptiles and amphibians, 42 of them species at risk. Maple and oak grow on warm south-facing slopes and hemlock in cool shaded ravines; there are cedar savannah, meadows and restored wetlands. Beavers work the creeks, coyotes live in the valleys, and black bears have been sighted in recent years.

People have lived along the Rouge for more than 10,000 years, and the park holds some of Canada's oldest known Indigenous sites. Its valleys carried travel routes used since time immemorial. Ten First Nations with historic and cultural ties to the area, including the seven Williams Treaties First Nations, the Mississaugas of the Credit, Six Nations of the Grand River and the Wendat Nation, sit on the park's First Nations Advisory Circle. European settlers arrived in 1799; the Mast Trail follows a logging route where pines were cut and floated downriver for shipbuilding, and orchards, mills and old cottage grounds survive in the woods.

Farming is part of what the park protects. More than 60 farmers work about 9,000 acres of the park, including prime Class 1 farmland, and the Rouge was the first federal protected area in Canada to protect agriculture. The park grew from more than 50 years of citizen campaigning to save the valley. The federal government committed to it in 2011, the Rouge National Urban Park Act came into force on 15 May 2015, and over the following years Transport Canada, Ontario, the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority and the City of Pickering transferred lands to Parks Canada; the park now spans more than 79 square kilometres.
howItWorks: Rouge is a national urban park, a different designation from a national park. Parks Canada describes a national urban park as a large, mostly natural area in or near a major city, formally designated by Parks Canada through a collaborative process, with three aims: conserving nature, connecting people with nature, and advancing reconciliation with Indigenous peoples. Unlike a national park, which is a federally administered protected area, a national urban park brings together several landowners and partners. Rouge has its own law, the Rouge National Urban Park Act, in force since 2015, and it includes leased farms, homes and businesses as well as natural areas. It was Canada's first national urban park; in 2021 the Government of Canada launched the National Urban Parks Program to build a network of them in the country's large urban centres.

There is no admission fee: the park is free and open 365 days a year, and its parking lots are open from 7:30 am to 9 pm and are locked overnight. Most Parks Canada national parks charge daily admission or accept the Parks Canada Discovery Pass, which in 2026 costs $83.50 for an adult, $71.50 for a senior and $167.50 for a family or group and covers more than 80 places for twelve months; neither is needed here. There are no campgrounds open to the public, no reservations for day visits, and no backcountry; groups should contact the park in advance, and events, commercial filming and research need a Parks Canada permit.

Park rules protect wildlife and farms alike. Do not approach, feed, collect or capture wildlife, or disturb nests, dens and dams; keep at least 100 metres from black bears and report sightings to Ontario's Bear Wise line. Pets must be under physical control at all times. No fires of any kind are allowed — no campfires, charcoal barbecues, candles or stoves — and hunting, drones, snowmobiles and off-road vehicles are prohibited. Stay on official trails and keep out of farm fields, buildings and other leased land. Fishing is allowed with a valid Ontario fishing licence under provincial rules, but taking crayfish out of the park is illegal.

sights.name: Vista Trail
sights.note: A 1.5-kilometre trail to a two-level viewing platform over the Little Rouge Creek and Rouge River valleys, one of the best places to see Toronto's autumn colours.

sights.name: Mast Trail
sights.note: A 2.5-kilometre route over a wooded ridge on a 200-year-old logging road, with rare Carolinian forest; it links Glen Rouge with Twyn Rivers Drive.

sights.name: Glen Eagles Vista
sights.note: A short trail to views of the Rouge River and Little Rouge Creek and a provincially significant bluff of sediments 13,000 to 30,000 years old. Parking closed November to May.

sights.name: Cedar Trail and Beare Wetlands
sights.note: A 4.5-kilometre loop from restored wetlands with snapping turtles and waterbirds up into cedar forest above Little Rouge Creek. Access from Zoo Road was closed in 2026.

sights.name: Rouge Marsh and Rouge Beach
sights.note: Toronto's largest remaining marsh and a sand beach at the river mouth on Lake Ontario, with a pedestrian bridge. Closed for construction since November 2025.

sights.name: Woodland Trail
sights.note: A 3.5-kilometre walk along the Rouge River through forest and meadow, known for beavers, past traces of a cottage area flooded by Hurricane Hazel in 1954.

sights.name: Bob Hunter Memorial Park
sights.note: Trailhead for the Monarch Trail through rare cedar savannah and the Tallgrass Trek past restored wetlands and meadows, named for the environmental campaigner Bob Hunter.

sights.name: Harvest Trail
sights.note: A 5.1-kilometre family trail through crop fields, marsh and woodlots in the park's farmland, between the 19th Avenue and Black Walnut day-use areas.

planYourVisit.reservations: No reservations are needed for a day visit, and the park is free. Groups are asked to contact the park in advance on 416-264-2020 or rouge@pc.gc.ca. Free guided walks run with Parks Canada staff and volunteers. Parking is limited and lots can close in bad weather — check live parking and bulletins before you go with Parks Canada.
permits: An Ontario fishing licence for anglers aged 18 to 64
A Parks Canada permit for events, commercial filming and photography, and research or collecting
camping: No public campground is listed in the park; the Learn-to Camp programme has ended
lodging: Accommodation across the Greater Toronto Area
seasonalClosures: Rouge Beach and Marsh and the Zoo Road Day Use Area were closed for construction in 2026, cutting the northern access to the Vista and Orchard trails
Glen Eagles Vista parking lot is closed from 1 November to 1 May
Trails are not salted or cleared of ice and snow in winter
Parts of the Monarch Trail were closed in November 2026 for erosion repairs — check before you go

weather: The Rouge has the four distinct seasons of southern Ontario. Spring brings migrating birds and, with snowmelt and heavy rain, the risk of sudden rises on the Rouge River; Parks Canada advises checking the conservation authority's flood messages before a visit. In the warmer months visitors paddle the river and marsh. Autumn colour is at its best from late September to mid-October, seen best from the Vista Trail platform and Glen Eagles Vista. In winter the trails stay open but are not salted or cleared, and the river ice is never safe to walk on.
directions: The park is in the east of the Greater Toronto Area, with many entrances in Toronto, Markham, Pickering and Uxbridge. Glen Rouge is about 36 kilometres from downtown Toronto by the Don Valley Parkway and Highway 401 to Kingston Road. By transit, take TTC Line 2 east to Kennedy Station and GO bus 92 towards Sheppard Avenue East and Kingston Road, then walk about 900 metres; or take the GO Lakeshore East train to Rouge Hill station, which is a 10–15 minute walk along the Waterfront Trail from Rouge Beach. Northern areas such as Bob Hunter Memorial Park are reached from Highway 401 by Meadowvale Road. Cycling to the park involves busy roads. Paddlers can launch at Glen Rouge and paddle down to Rouge Marsh in about an hour.

fees.title: Admission and parking
fees.detail: The park is free and open 365 days a year; parking at the day-use areas is free but limited. As stated by Parks Canada in November 2026.

chronology.text: People are living in the Rouge Valley; some of Canada's oldest known Indigenous sites lie in the park.
European settlers arrive in the Rouge Valley.
Hurricane Hazel floods the cottage and camping area along the river at Woodland.
In the Speech from the Throne on 3 June, the Government of Canada commits to creating a national urban park in the Rouge Valley.
What becomes the park's First Nations Advisory Circle is established on 5 July.
The Rouge National Urban Park Act receives Royal Assent on 23 April and comes into force on 15 May, creating Canada's first national urban park.
Amendments to the Act receive Royal Assent on 19 June, strengthening ecological protection and affirming the role of park farmers.
The park's first management plan is tabled in Parliament in January; in September the first Parks Canada-built facilities open, the Black Walnut and 19th Avenue day-use areas and the Harvest Trail.
Parks Canada launches the National Urban Parks Program to create a network of national urban parks.
The park marks ten years since its establishment.

safety: The Rouge River can rise quickly in heavy rain or snowmelt. Stay out of the water after storms, never walk on river ice, and take care near water at all times.
Swimming at Rouge Beach is not recommended: water quality varies and bacteria levels may be a health risk, and there are no lifeguards.

Black bears have been seen in the park. Keep at least 100 metres away, never approach or corner one, keep dogs leashed, and call 911 if anyone is in danger. Coyotes are usually shy; if one approaches, back away slowly and make yourself big and loud.
Some trails are steep, there is no food or water at trailheads, and cycling to and between areas often means riding on busy roads. In an emergency call 911.
regulations: Do not approach, feed, collect or capture wildlife, or disturb nests, dens and dams.
No fires of any kind, including campfires, charcoal barbecues and candles.
Pets must be under physical control; clean up after them.
No hunting, firearms, fireworks, drones, snowmobiles or off-road vehicles.
Stay on official trails and off farm fields and other leased land; do not pick crops or plants, and do not remove crayfish.
